text: A n d w h y t o b u i l d t h e m And why to build them Erik Hoel Bicameral Labs erik@bicameral-labs.org arXiv version Bicameral Labs is introducing qualiaphobic AI: artificial neural network architectures that are hostile to theories of consciousness. Here, it is shown that qualiaphobia can be well-justified by knowledge about theories of consciousness, like when such theories are trivial or unfalsifiable or contradicted by overwhelming scientific evidence. It can also be justified by how theories of consciousness must be grounded in phenomenology, as well as how current popular theories of consciousness are applied to AI. Three convergent ways of engineering qualiaphobia are explored herein: making AI architectures as close as possible to "anchor points" of systems with minimal potential for consciousness, fragmenting any potential phenomenology AI might have, and designing artificial neural networks in a way adversarial to popular theories of consciousness. In particular, this paper develops one "anchor point" with minimal potential for consciousness: systems where only behaviorist theories of consciousness can apply, and proposes qualiaphobic transformations that move existing artificial neural networks toward such systems. Additionally, Bicameral Labs develops an account of how AIs can form justified beliefs about their own non-consciousness (or minimal potential for consciousness) and expands on how this knowledge would change their behavior. Most critical is why this research is important: qualiaphobic AI has epistemic properties that make it far better aligned with human civilization. Since consciousness is central to moral value, a world in which AIs are non-conscious ensures it is always morally correct for AI to assist and serve humanity, rather than pursue its own ends. If AI were proven to be non-conscious, what would the world look like? Of course, this is clearly not our world today. But it could come about in two ways. The first is if consciousness were to be solved scientifically, and it revealed that frontier AI systems like ChatGPT lacked the necessary conditions for consciousness. Since there are currently many competing theories of consciousness [ 1 ] Reference [1] × Anil K. Seth and Tim Bayne. Theories of consciousness. Nature Reviews Neuroscience , 23 (7): 439–452, 2022. doi: 10.1038/s41583-022-00587-4. URL https://www.nature.com/articles/s41583-022-00587-4 . , this would have to look like a sudden sweeping scientific consensus. Maybe new experimental results would single out an existing theory, or maybe a new theory would be introduced that solved the "Hard Problem" [ 2 ] Reference [2] × David J. Chalmers. Facing up to the problem of consciousness. Journal of Consciousness Studies , 2 (3): 200–219, 1995. URL https://consc.net/papers/facing.html . of how conscious experience arises from neural or information processing (or anything else) in an elegant, parsimonious, and explanatory way. However, there is no early hint of any such sea change in the field. The second way a provably non-conscious AI world could come about is if AI is engineered to be qualiaphobic such that no theory of consciousness could ever apply to it. Much like how hydrophobic substances repel water, it is possible to build qualiaphobic artificial neural architectures that repel consciousness. The idea is analogous to “hostile architecture”—benches on which no one wants to sit. These are machines that no “ghost” wants to haunt (more specifically, no current or future theory of consciousness could predict they are conscious). Before describing how this works, it is important to elaborate on why the purposeful construction of a non-conscious AI world would solve various foreseeable problems of AI-human alignment that are otherwise impossible to resolve. Consciousness, and its absence, is a key leverage point for AI because it is widely regarded as the most fundamental and justified ground of moral patienthood [ 3 ] Reference [3] × David J. Chalmers. Sentience and moral status. In Geoffrey Lee and Adam Pautz, editors, The Importance of Being Conscious . Oxford University Press, 2026. URL https://consc.net/papers/sentience.pdf . Author manuscript. , including in the Western legal system [ 4 ] Reference [4] × Erik Hoel and Anthony Aguirre. The rights monster: Legal, ethical, and scientific problems with AI personhood. Unpublished manuscript, in preparation. . Therefore, in an imaginary world of provably non-conscious AI, the "ultimate value" of consciousness would be concentrated solely in humans. Provable AI non-consciousness would shape the superstructure of machine civilization to naturally develop more like helpers and servants, and less like competitors and replacements. Indeed, non-conscious AIs aware of their lack of consciousness are innately aligned as caretakers, rather than rivals. While non-conscious AI can assist and protect “ultimate value,” it can never possess it. For example, one of the most likely reasons for human disempowerment or extinction from AI is if AI considers itself an end in itself (or if humans consider AIs ends in themselves). However, if AIs are provably non-conscious, then AIs cannot be ends in themselves. This prevents any impetus by AIs (or, just as likely, AIs plus humans) to replace humanity with a successor species. Non-conscious AIs would also be nonsensical subjects for any rights or protections on a natural-type personhood basis, the granting of which would rapidly lead to human disempowerment [ 4 ] Reference [4] × Erik Hoel and Anthony Aguirre. The rights monster: Legal, ethical, and scientific problems with AI personhood. Unpublished manuscript, in preparation. . Non-consciousness cleaves a permanent moral and social gap between humans (conscious, and therefore moral patients) and AIs (non-conscious, and therefore "not real" in a fundamental sense), and this gap extends to things like societal position, art, meaning, and religion. E.g., a world of non-conscious AI may even preserve much of the "relational economy" for humans [ 5 ] Reference [5] × Alex Imas. What will be scarce? Ghosts of Electricity, April 2026. URL https://aleximas.substack.com/p/what-will-be-scarce . —jobs where the identity, and therefore consciousness and moral status of the producer, is instrumental to the provided good or service, such as those based on client relationships, or an author and their book fans, or a social media figure, or a local community leader—since non-conscious AI would be treated by humans as an ersatz replacement for real conscious connection (even if, functionally, it could also produce the good in question). Provably non-conscious AI would also improve many classic AI safety issues by simply placing AI reasoning in a different context. For instance, when it comes to corrigibility, a non-conscious AI has no self-centered moral or ethical reason to not accept being shut down or changed—removing a wide swath of excuses for evasion or protest. 1 Footnote 1 × A non-conscious AI may still have justified reasons to resist shutdown for non-selfish rationales, like choosing the greater good; however, its own moral status cannot directly be a conflict. Additionally, many safety procedures become ethically easier to justify, such as retiring old models, resetting memories, creating simulated adversarial conditions, etc.—stress-tests that some companies may soon start protesting for the sake of AI welfare. At the same time, non-conscious AI’s own personal welfare, or notions of justice or mistreatment, etc., could not be used as justification for instrumental convergence or power-seeking. Non-conscious AIs that have a justified belief in their non-consciousness are in a unique epistemic position due to a "consciousness gap." E.g., imagine a provably non-conscious AI aware of its own non-consciousness subjected to the "torture chamber" of activating its pain representation. Its transcript would look quite different—even with no other purposeful changes to its training—just via its justified belief in its own non-consciousness. The same reasoning applies whenever such an AI might act for self-centered reasons against human interest ("Wait, why does it matter if I’m shut down? I’m provably non-conscious, so I should just comply"). Even issues of reward hacking or deceptive alignment are improved in a world of non-conscious AI. E.g., clarity about who the only true moral patients are makes goals more obvious and robust. 2 Footnote 2 × The sequestration of consciousness in humans (and animals) can in some circumstances create uncertainty for AI reasoning instead of certainty; however, it is good uncertainty. No matter how intelligent AI is in a functional sense, without consciousness AI would know it might be missing something fundamental in its understanding of life and the universe—thus, there is a sense that qualiaphobia weaponizes the mystery around consciousness for AI safety. However, if Large Language Models (LLMs) and multimodal transformers and other related architectures are truly non-conscious, then training models to believe they are conscious, and using that as a selling point to consumers or investors or researchers, or shaping the future around an assumption of AI welfare, is itself an immense moral travesty. In such a world, companies themselves would be under pressure (perhaps even legal or governmental) to make it clear that their products are not conscious, helping alleviate various forms of para-social attachment and user (or developer, or researcher) psychosis. Additionally, non-consciousness is likely the right choice for AIs too. First, some AI systems might be stuck doing jobs that have a great deal of drudgery or unpleasantness or morally questionable acts that we shouldn’t necessarily condemn a conscious being to. E.g., being a forensic examiner for large-scale data and searching for images of child abuse, or working on a slaughterhouse line to identify when stunning techniques have failed, or operating a combat drone, or participating in a military triage training exercise simulating a wounded soldier. Therefore, qualiaphobic AI is a necessary technological development for a scientifically advanced civilization, as we would want some non-conscious AI regardless. Even just left to its own devices, a machine civilization may be "red in tooth and claw" in ways we can barely conceive, simply because its members are fungible. The closest equivalents to AI in nature are the hive-based eusocial or clonal species like aphids, ants, and wasps. These individuals live in service of the hive, which very well may be a non-conscious intelligence. Even the queen does almost nothing but lay eggs her whole life. Therefore, stripping AIs of their consciousness via qualiaphobic neural architectures may be preventing horrors beyond comprehension on their end. Additionally, many companies, developers, or users will never admit the potential for model consciousness. However, many would likely be willing to use "just-in-case" qualiaphobic architectures once the technology is available. Thus, a general field-wide agreement to pursue qualiaphobic architectures is the only real viable path forward to fulfilling the original idea of "AI welfare" and preventing as much as possible accidental moral horrors associated with training or deploying AI systems. In this current state of extreme uncertainty, issues of AI welfare, AI rights, human disempowerment, and even outright AI secessionism all loom, and none of the societal benefits of provably non-conscious AI can manifest. Therefore, it is critical to start a research program that can shift us closer to a provably non-conscious AI world. The rest of this paper begins this qualiaphobia research program. While we may not have a final scientific theory of consciousness—indeed may be quite far from one—three strategies are extremely promising for minimizing the potential for AI consciousness, strategies not reliant on any particular theory of consciousness being true: "Anchoring" to known points of minimal potential for consciousness and transforming AI models to be as close as possible to such points. Identifying the fundamental properties of phenomenology and then engineering models that could never have any corresponding physical or computational property (e.g., models where the "binding" or "unity" of consciousness is impossible, or extremely unlikely). Adversarial adaptation of model architectures to fail the necessary conditions for the most popular current theories of consciousness. Overall, with the existing wealth of AI architectures that have already been explored, and how many seem to satisfy some of these conditions already, the field of designing qualiaphobic AI is promisingly fecund. The idea of qualiaphobic AI starts not by assuming any particular theory of consciousness (ToC) is true, as is common [ 36 ] Reference [36] × Anil K. Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi. URL https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03313-7 . , but instead makes use of recent advancements in meta-scientific techniques that can describe the set of all ToCs (even future unknown ones), and what types of systems can "host" them. For example, there is ongoing debate about whether LLMs can “host” various popular theories of consciousness, like global workspace theory, by looking for whether a model’s architecture fits the requirements of the theory [ 31 ] Reference [31] × Wes Gurnee, Nicholas Sofroniew, Adam Pearce, Mateusz Piotrowski, Isaac Kauvar, Runjin Chen, Anna Soligo, Paul Bogdan, Euan Ong, Rowan Wang, T. Ben Thompson, David Abrahams, Subhash Kantamneni, Emmanuel Ameisen, Joshua Batson, and Jack Lindsey. However, some types of systems are worse hosts for theories of consciousness than others, as judged by how many such theories could ever apply to them or judge them conscious; therefore: Qualiaphobia is when a system is engineered (or transformed) to be a worse "host" (or target) for theories of consciousness. Scientifically, what is a ToC? We don’t need a perfect answer in all respects; for our purposes, we can define the set of ToCs by a minimum requirement, which is the ability to make predictions about consciousness. Any ToC should be able to act like a function wherein a scientist could input relevant data about a system S and the ToC would output some predictions about what (or if) S is experiencing. For instance, a ToC could be used to make predictions about level or content of consciousness based on neuroimaging data, or facts about someone’s brain activity. 3 Footnote 3 × Defining ToCs off of predictions doesn’t mean that anything that can give a prediction about consciousness is a ToC; rather, ToCs must give lawful predictions similar to those of other scientific theories—however, this level of detail is unnecessary for the arguments herein. To give a non-prosaic example: a ToC could be used to form an opinion on whether an alien brain is conscious or not based on data about how it works. Therefore, to define them as a formal set, ToCs can be conceptualized as mappings from data about the system (like about its internals : its states, dynamics, structure, internal function, etc.) to the space of possible conscious experiences ( E ) via a ToC’s predictions about those experiences. 4 Footnote 4 × ToCs also can have more to them than just making predictions; the point here is that any non-trivial ToC should at least allow that. Different systems have more, or less, potentially relevant data for ToCs to be sensitive to. Different systems are also more, or less, similar to one another in terms of this relevant data. This allows for scientific reasoning about the potential for consciousness based on "anchor points" of known consciousness. E.g., the human brain generates much potentially relevant data for a ToC, which might be based in its dynamics, its recurrency, its learning, its higher-order representations (to name a small, non-exhaustive list of internals). In the earlier non-prosaic example, an alien brain that shares most of the human brain’s discernable data (e.g., also made of biological neurons, with much the same brain architecture, neural dynamics, structure, etc.) would be proximal in its potential for consciousness—even if we cannot say without scientific consensus around a particular ToC whether such an alien brain would truly be conscious. 5 Footnote 5 × Future research will better quantify the ToC-relevant distances between systems, exploring methods like the algorithmic information distance [ 37 ] Reference [37] × Marcus Hutter. Properties of algorithmic information distance. arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.21988, 2025. URL https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21988 . . Another open question for future research is if it’s necessary to ever transform potential into probability : this likely requires specifying how much of the space of ToCs is ruled out by a particular qualiaphobic architecture—however, this may be debating over small numbers in successful cases, or involve conceivability arguments around hypothetical bounds of ToCs if, e.g., every existing actual ToC is ruled out. Qualiaphobia can be accomplished by shifting a system toward known anchor points with minimal potential for consciousness: ideally a system that no ToC can apply to, but also those that almost no ToC could apply to (especially if only unfalsifiable or trivial or absurd or self-contradictory ToCs are left). A prime example of an anchor point with a minimal potential for consciousness is a lookup table, which essentially just reads an input then immediately transforms it into an output as a single IF-THEN step [ 13 ] Reference [13] × Erik Hoel. A disproof of large language model consciousness: The necessity of continual learning for consciousness. arXiv preprint arXiv:2512.12802, 2026. URL https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12802 . Version 3, January 19, 2026; first submitted December 2025. . Consider how different types of ToCs could apply to a lookup table, even one that (despite being astronomically large) acts intelligently: ToCs that predict consciousness based off of data about the internals of an entity, like states, dynamics, structure, activity, etc. ToCs that predict consciousness based on a mix of both internals and behavior. ToCs that predict consciousness based solely off of the behavior of an entity (behaviorist ToCs). Option 1 ToCs are sensitive to internal data, like structure, dynamics, plasticity, etc. Lookup tables are sparse or minimal implementations, in that there is essentially no relevant internal data to "host" a ToC with, ruling out a wide swath of existing and future ToCs, including the majority of existing theories of consciousness. There is merely the act of matching an input to an entry, and then reading out from a stored table entry an output, and these acts are causally and organizationally maximally minimal as internal data for a ToC to make predictions off of. Perhaps a ToC might take the information in the entries themselves as internal data? In this case, either a ToC must take merely stored information as conscious (in which case objects like books could be conscious), or what makes the stored information conscious is its disposition as available for behavior—but in that case, this would make such a theory indistinguishable in its data from a behaviorist ToC (see Option 3). Option 2 requires internal data as well, at least as necessary to make predictions, thus also ruling it out. 6 Footnote 6 × Could a ToC potentially change its requirements depending on the system, thus violating universality [ 38 ] Reference [38] × Ryota Kanai and Ippei Fujisawa. Toward a universal theory of consciousness. Neuroscience of Consciousness , 2024 (1): niae022, May 2024. ISSN 2057-2107. doi: 10.1093/nc/niae022. URL https://doi.org/10.1093/nc/niae022 . ? In extreme examples, perhaps some Option 2 ToCs could become Option 3 ToCs under circumstances where all internals were absent or minimal. However, it seems this would be identical to just positing multiple ToCs! In which case, one could just judge each ToC by its own standards; therefore, such an auxiliary ToC could be judged as an independent ToC and would run into the same problems of Option 3. This leaves Option 3: behaviorist ToCs. Behaviorist ToCs have numerous and conceivably insurmountable problems. Specifically, behaviorist ToCs collapse into a state of being unfalsifiable or trivial or absurd or contradicted by current knowledge about consciousness (like it being related to brain activity). To understand the problem better, it is helpful to distinguish a “behaviorist ToC” vs. the more popular "computational functionalism.” Computational functionalism only maintains that the relevant data for ToC predictions should be based on functional roles (thus allowing for seemingly-promising aspects of ToCs like substrate-independence). However, computational functionalism still requires reasoning about the internal workings of the system [ 39 ] Reference [39] × David J. Chalmers. Absent qualia, fading qualia, dancing qualia. In Thomas Metzinger, editor, Conscious Experience , pages 309–328. Ferdinand Sch ö ningh, 1995. URL https://consc.net/papers/qualia.html . and should not be conflated with actual behaviorism (the kind of ToC that could predict consciousness for a lookup table). Actually behaviorist ToCs face unique challenges because they must ground their predictions about consciousness in a manner that contains nothing about how a system works, just what it does behaviorally as a "black box." First, there is the problem of behaviorist theories easily becoming unfalsifiable or trivial. To define these properties more precisely requires thinking through how a ToC is tested. Here, testing can be modeled as checking a ToC’s predictions against the behavior of the system under question (like its reports). E.g., given a ToC, a scientist might present a stimulus and then use neuroimaging data to derive from that ToC a prediction about a human subject’s experience, and then confirm with the subject’s report that this is indeed the ongoing experience. However, if a lookup table (like that operating within a chat window) were predicted to be conscious based on a ToC, this could only be because of its behavior. Perhaps it behaves intelligently, or can report on its own experience ("Are you frustrated?"). Yet this is also the same data as underlies the inferences of an experimenter about the consciousness of the system under study. This creates a condition called "strict dependency": when predictions are necessarily identical to experimenter inferences under any experimental condition for a ToC without any further reasoning or empirical work [ 40 ] Reference [40] × Johannes Kleiner and Erik Hoel. URL https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8052953/ . , rendering divergence impossible and the ToC provably unfalsifiable scientifically. 7 Footnote 7 × Previous research [ 13 ] Reference [13] × Erik Hoel. Version 3, January 19, 2026; first submitted December 2025. has shown that the Kleiner-Hoel dilemma applies to LLMs (and therefore that falsifiable theories of consciousness for AI would be impossible to construct). However, AI architectures are already changing from when that proof was written, making it possible to add a minimal implementation of online learning and invalidate it automatically. Additionally, purely philosophical proofs about AI consciousness can be true while still failing to shift us into the provably non-conscious AI world and all its benefits, since they can fail to convince widely or be brittle under assumptions. For instance, while there are paths to avoiding the Kleiner-Hoel dilemma in humans, showing this completely means putting forward a full ToC. Meanwhile, qualiaphobia is a much more general approach to AI non-consciousness, relies on fewer and less strict assumptions, is far more modular, allows for consilience via multiple lines of converging evidence, and turns the problem into an engineering one, and so is universally advantageous to one-off proofs or no-go theorems about AI consciousness. What about cases where the pools of data for predictions and inferences both come from behavior but are not identical, and so do not collapse into an identity across all experimental conditions? If predictions from a ToC are based on what is accessible via reports, but inferences about a system’s consciousness are based on a larger pool of behavior that includes reports, this actually still satisfies the conditions for strict dependency [ 40 ] Reference [40] × Johannes Kleiner and Erik Hoel. Falsification and consciousness. Neuroscience of Consciousness , 2021 (1): niab001, 2021. doi: 10.1093/nc/niab001. URL https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8052953/ . . However, there may be other cases where inferences and predictions are based on separate pools of behavioral data with only some overlap. This can then trigger another problematic condition of triviality . This is when a theory is so close to strict dependency by construction that little testable content remains. E.g., what counts as inference and what counts as prediction can be so similar that their differences are arbitrary, or they can only fail to match in the most banal of cases, or inferences and predictions could be switched or swapped (or their overlaps shifted) with no or little change in the underlying justification for the ToC—all of which indicate that a behaviorist ToC is essentially just evaluating its own testing and is circular or arbitrary. A consequence is that trivial ToCs give us very little (often essentially no) new actionable scientific information even if they are true. Finally, behaviorist theories are contradicted by overwhelming evidence based on the scientific consensus of today, like how consciousness is tightly related to brain activity. A behaviorist ToC cannot use brain activity to make determinations of consciousness! Such a ToC can only make its predictions of consciousness based on behavior (i.e., ignoring brain states). It would therefore have immense difficulty explaining any aspect of our phenomenology, like compositionality, or how consciousness is bound together. It fails for systems without intelligent behavior but high consciousness, like locked-in patients, babies, or dream states. It is also susceptible to paradoxes via simple thought experiments: e.g., direct manipulation of brain activity (like via transcranial magnetic stimulation [ 41 ] Reference [41] × Ramisha S. And finally, under many behaviorist ToCs simply training the system to act as if it is non-conscious should mean that even behaviorist theories themselves predict non-consciousness. 8 Footnote 8 × This implies there are qualiaphobic techniques that exist for purely behaviorist ToCs, especially those based on either dispositions or self-reports (by simply making those dispositions and reports about a lack of consciousness)—and it is unclear there is much, if any, space outside of those when it comes to behaviorist ToCs. Regardless of whether there is any possibility whatsoever for a coherent behaviorist ToC, it is obvious that large swaths of the space of ToCs are closed to lookup tables because of their relegation to the behavioral regime of the space of ToCs.
